https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.title: Queen's bedroom intruder Michael Fagan: I don't regret it
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.subtitle: Mr Fagan's break-in is dramatised in the new series of The Crown with Olivia Colman
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.text:
The man who broke into the Queen’s bedroom in the Royal Family’s most infamous security breach has said he does not regret it.
The incident is dramatised in the new series of The Crown, revisiting a story that made headlines around the world in 1982.
Michael Fagan, an out-of-work painter and decorator, climbed the railings at Buckingham Palace, shinned up a drainpipe, got in through an open window and wandered the corridors, eventually finding himself face-to-face with the monarch.
Speaking ahead of the drama’s release this Sunday, Mr Fagan said: “There’s plenty of people who’ve knelt before the Queen but there’s not many who’ve sat on her bed and had a chat, is there?”
The Telegraph tracked down Mr Fagan, who is now 70 and recovering from a recent heart attack and the after-effects of covid, to a tower block in Islington, north London.
Peter Morgan, the Netflix writer, did not approach him to contribute to the programme. The screen conversation between Mr Fagan (played by Tom Brooke) and the Queen (Olivia Colman) is a work of fiction.
In fact, despite reports at the time that Mr Fagan engaged the monarch in a 10-minute chat, very few words were actually exchanged.
“I pulled back the curtain and she said, ‘What are you doing here?’” Her tone, he said, was not as clipped as he had expected. “She talks like me and you, normal. Well, I sound a bit common so maybe not like that. But very normal.”
The Queen did not, as the show cheekily suggests, address Mr Fagan with her favoured line in small talk: “Have you come far?”
In reality, after a short moment in which Mr Fagan sat on the bed, she told him, “I’ll be back in a minute,” and darted out of the room. “She walked out on her little legs. Then a footman comes in and goes, ‘You look like you need a drink, mate.’”
The footman, Paul Whybrew, took Mr Fagan down the corridor. “He pours me a whisky out of the pantry. Then the policemen came and they were all over the place - they hadn’t arrested anyone for years, they were on a retirement posting, on guard duty. One of them was fumbling around for his notebook.”
Until the Queen sat up and spoke, Mr Fagan had not realised it was her bedroom as he did not think it grand enough to belong to a monarch. “She never had a four-poster bed. And she’s got a little thing where she does her teas and coffees.”
The Netflix drama suggests that Mr Fagan launched a diatribe about Baroness Thatcher, telling the Queen that the Prime Minister had ruined the country. In reality, he said, that was not the case and Morgan had “used a lot of artistic licence”; he still has no explanation for why he broke in, although he was frustrated by joblessness and the break-up of his marriage.
But he conceded that he did share the anti-Thatcher sentiment. “A lot of people thought like that. She did a lot of damage to children. She was like Trump,” he said.
Mr Fagan was arrested but not charged with trespass, as it was then a civil offence. Incredibly, it was the second time he had broken into the Palace - on the first, he was disturbed by a maid and fled. He was latterly charged with stealing a bottle of wine during that first intrusion, but was acquitted.
He was, however, sent to a psychiatric hospital for three months before returning home. In 1997, he was jailed for four years for heroin offences. Now he lives with his partner of 17 years, Rhian, and has three great-grandchildren.
The Crown will bring him renewed attention but he plans to take it in his stride. He has always been well-known character in his local area, he said, and enjoys his small place in royal history. “I’ve met children downstairs who say, ‘We were learning about you in our lessons.’ Kids get taught about me at school, I swear,” he said.
In the drama, the fictional catalyst for the Palace break-in is a meeting with his unsympathetic MP, a Tory who sarcastically suggests that Mr Fagan take his concerns about the state of the country to the Queen.
Perhaps Netflix missed a trick with the MP’s depiction. As an Islington resident, Mr Fagan’s MP is Jeremy Corbyn
author: Anita Singh

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.title: What makes a good Prime Minister? See the big picture – and have complete control of your advisers
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.subtitle: From Robert Walpole to Theresa May, history has provided plenty of lessons on what Boris Johnson should and shouldn't do as PM
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.text:
What makes a great prime minister? There’s no science to it and the qualities we describe as “great” inevitably change over generations.
The role has been brought into sharp focus over the past few days with the departure of Boris Johnson’s two closest advisers, the continuing saga of the EU free trade talks and the ongoing Covid crisis. All prime ministers are leaders, of course, but how they exercise that leadership determines what kind of legacy they leave – a fact Boris is all too aware of.
The demands of the job in 1721 were very different to those of a 21st century premiership. How would Sir Robert Walpole have coped with the demands of the 24-hour news media? How would Lloyd George have handled the potential loss of the American colonies? Would William Gladstone have navigated the pandemic better?
We will never know, but perhaps now is a good time to reflect, given next year marks the 300th anniversary of the office of PM. It’s why I have written a book, The Prime Ministers, to celebrate the lives of the 55 men and women who have held it in Britain – from the unknown Earl of Shelburne to giants like Margaret Thatcher and Winston Churchill – and evaluate where they fit into the pantheon of great, or not so great PMs.
Perhaps the greatest accolade ever accorded to a prime minister was Punch’s judgment on Gladstone: “Had he been a worse man, he would have been a better politician.” The truth – although voters are reluctant to accept it – is that politicians are just like anyone else, with the same flaws and frailties. Gladstone, who served a record four terms between 1868 and 1894, was a classic example of a man who wanted to be perfect, but ended up self flagellating over illicit thoughts he had about the fallen women he and Mrs Gladstone had invited into their home to “save”.
Yet he was a prime minister full of self-knowledge. He knew his weaknesses and compensated for them. With age comes wisdom. Given today’s band of ever younger prime ministers, one wonders if the same can be said of Tony Blair, David Cameron or Boris Johnson.
In the 18th and 19th centuries, PMs were in part judged by their leadership in military conflict, but that has also been the case for recent PMs like Blair and Thatcher.
Asquith lost his job in 1916 because he didn’t have the qualities of a war leader. Lloyd George did, and the Conservatives recognised it and put him into Number Ten. Overnight, momentum in the First World War was transformed.
However, a successful warrior does not necessarily a great prime minister make. One of the greatest Britons of the 19th century, the Duke of Wellington, had huge successes as a military commander, but as a politician he arguably failed to change the climate. He was not transformational in the way that his successor, Earl Grey was. Grey not only gave his name to a tea, he passed the 1832 Reform Act and abolished slavery. Quite a legacy.
A successful PM must not let themselves get bogged down in the detail. Both Gordon Brown and Theresa May fell into that trap, with the result that decisions were delayed and the Downing Street machine often ground to a halt.
An ability to stand back and see the big picture is also a real asset. Harold Macmillan rarely involved himself in detail, but set a direction of travel. He and Stanley Baldwin were good examples of prime ministers who paced themselves so that they had spare capacity to deal with the unexpected and the urgent.
As Mayor of London, Boris Johnson took a hands-off approach. He recognised his own weaknesses and appointed people to compensate for them. Over time, that approach worked. Sir Simon Milton became his chief consigliere, and ensured that mayoral policy was carried out. In Number Ten, the same role was ceded to Dominic Cummings. Where Sir Simon brought people together and cajoled them into action, Cummings took a more disruptive approach - with the inevitable consequences we saw last week.
Having control of your advisers is an absolute requisite for success. And history tells us that when they start to become the story, it’s probably time to look for new advisers. I’m sure Alastair Campbell would agree.
Good PMs can also draw ministers into their mindset. They inspire trust, and just as importantly give it. Harold Wilson was a good, sometimes far-sighted prime minister but he was paranoid. He saw a plot against him around every corner. In some ways he was a consummate manager of his own party, and saw off any real challenge to his authority, as any competent prime minister must do. Once prime ministers had to maintain the patronage and support of the monarch - woe betide them if the King took against them. Nowadays, lose the support of your parliamentary party and you’re toast.
You also need a good mind or good intuition – preferably both – to be a truly great PM. Underrated is the ability to listen and understand where others are coming from. Most of the time you need to be a team leader, but the greatest of all seem to know when it is necessary to be the chief.
The team usually wants to be led. That’s what inspires loyalty and devotion. Theresa May flummoxed her Cabinet by allowing them all a say, but then refused to make her own position clear. Ministers left Cabinet meetings with no clear idea of what had been decided. It was a recipe for her eventual fall.
To be prime minister for any but a short period you have got to be able to win elections and to win elections you need to have an instinctive connection with key electoral groups. Thatcher and Blair both had that in spades. They didn’t just appeal to their own party’s core voters, they attracted those who had traditionally voted for their opponents. Big parliamentary majorities enabled them to change the political weather. Too few prime ministers have the character or ability to do that.
There are personality cults around most prime ministers who win elections. That was as true of Walpole and Pitt the Younger as of Churchill, Thatcher and Blair. It is not, however, true of perhaps the greatest Labour prime minister of all, Clement Attlee. Attlee could never become PM today, being so averse to any form of communication through the written or broadcast media.
It is also no accident that every dominant and long serving prime minister from Walpole to Pitt had also been Chancellor of the Exchequer. Prime ministers not competent and trusted with the national economy, and especially with taxation, soon fall – as do prime ministers who fall out with their Chancellors, or don’t have the political power to rein them in.
Politicians who exude optimism often make their own luck. Others are just plain lucky. Some, like Pitt, Thatcher and Blair were lucky to have such ineffective opponents. Others just happened to be in the right place at the right time. Unfortunately for Neville Chamberlain, James Callaghan and, some might say, Boris Johnson, they had the bad luck to be in the wrong place at the wrong time. On such vagaries are prime ministerial reputations made.
The Prime Ministers by Iain Dale (RRP £25). Buy now for £19.99 at books.telegraph.co.uk or call 0844 871 1514

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.title: The attempt to censor Jordan Peterson shows the intolerance of the social justice generation
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.subtitle: The writer won't be the last victim of a new generation of 'progressives'
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.text:
It’s easy to forget what a recent phenomenon freedom of expression is, even in this country. Until 1959, British publishers could be sent to jail for producing books deemed to have “a tendency to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences”.
Back then, the things that couldn’t be said were largely sexual. James Joyce’s masterpiece, Ulysses, was banned – indeed burned – on the grounds of obscenity. A single line in Radclyffe Hall’s The Well of Loneliness (“And that night they were not divided”) convinced a magistrate that all copies must be destroyed, because it could “induce thoughts of a most impure character and would glorify the horrible tendency of lesbianism”.
The bravery of successive generations of publishers, their mischievous insistence on thumbing their nose at the censors, helped bring about the sexual revolution, enabling us all to live and love – and read – more freely. The obscenity trial, 60 years ago, of Lady Chatterley’s Lover (or more accurately, of its publisher, Penguin Books), is widely recognised as the moment when the gates of artistic and sexual freedom were finally blown open.
Now, though, there are those who wish to drag them shut again. This time it isn’t the “grey elderly ones”, as Lawrence described his censors, having apoplexies over the written word. Today, the blue pencil hovers in the hand of young “progressives” – some of them, astonishingly, publishers themselves.
Staff at Penguin Random House tried this week to block the publication of a new book by Jordan Peterson, the Canadian academic whose contempt for identity politics has earned him a huge following on the Right. At a “town hall meeting” at Penguin’s Canada office, employees argued that the publisher should not give a “platform” to an “icon of hate speech”. According to one of those present, “people were crying in the meeting about how Mr Peterson has affected their lives”, with one employee fretting that the publication of the book would “negatively affect their non-binary friend”.
To Penguin’s great credit, it is pressing ahead with publication. But as the social justice generation moves up the media hierarchy, this bizarre sight – publishers protesting against their own publishing house for publishing a book – will only become more common.
Earlier this year, the US firm Hachette dropped its plans to publish Woody Allen’s memoirs after staff staged a walkout. The American journalist Abigail Shrier has described how her latest book, an investigation into the rise in transgender identification among adolescent girls, was dropped by her first publishers following protests by staff. When another publisher picked it up, newspapers refused to review it. When the podcaster Joe Rogan interviewed Shrier about her book, staff at Spotify, the podcast platform, threatened to walk out. Censorship is once more in the ascendant.
They are so easily rattled, these new inspectors of literary hygiene. No sensible critic of Peterson would claim that his books constitute hate speech. (Unlike Mein Kampf, which Penguin, quite rightly, continues to publish on the grounds of public interest.) The argument against Peterson seems to be that, even if he isn’t a neo-Nazi, some of his fans are. But since when did we judge a book by its readers?
If reading has any moral purpose, it is that it broadens our understanding of the world by exposing us to different ideas. This is what makes publishing an exalted profession: its whole purpose is to find ideas and set them free. A publisher should be a liberator, not a jailer.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.title: Celebrities including Rita Ora and Laurence Fox must follow restrictions, PM warns
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.subtitle: Boris Johnson's official spokesman says it is important that everyone, including celebrities, sets an example by obeying the rules
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.text:
Boris Johnson has intervened in the Rita Ora birthday party row, saying even celebrities have to stick to the coronavirus rules.
The Prime Minister's official spokesman said it was important that everyone, including celebrities, "set an example by following the rules".
His comments came as Ora faced the prospect of a £10,000 fine after organising a 30th birthday party in Notting Hill, west London, to which police were called over complaints that it was in breach of Covid regulations.
The pop star admitted the "small gathering" with friends to celebrate her birthday was an "inexcusable error of judgment".
In a post on her Instagram story, she said: "It was a spur of the moment decision made with the misguided view that we were coming out of lockdown and this would be OK. I'm deeply sorry for breaking the rules and in turn understand that this puts people at risk.
"Given the restrictions, I realise how irresponsible these actions were and I take full responsibility.
"I feel particularly embarrassed knowing first-hand how hard people have worked to combat this terrible illness and being fully aware of the sacrifices that people and businesses have made to help keep us all safe. Even though this won't make it right, I want to sincerely apologise."
The Prime Minister's spokesman said: "It's important that everybody in society sets an example by following the rules – that is for every member of the public, including celebrities."
"Throughout the pandemic we've been clear that it's vital for everyone to abide by the rules in order to suppress the virus and reduce the transmission, but enforcement is a matter for the police.
"The Prime Minister has been clear on the need for everybody across the country to continue to abide by the rules in order to reduce the transmission of the virus, but it's up to police to decide what action to take."
Scotland Yard confirmed that officers had been called to an address in Notting Hill, west London, on Saturday night amid a breach of Covid regulations. It declined to say whether any further action would be taken.
It came as actor Laurence Fox faced an online backlash over a tweet in which he claimed to have had people over for dinner and appeared to criticise the NHS.
"Just had a large group over to lunch and we hugged and ate and talked and put the world to rights," he wrote. "If the @nhs can't cope, then the @nhs isn't fit for purpose."

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.title: Turks hailed as heroes after they drag Vienna injured to safety
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.subtitle: Two immigrants risked their lives to save elderly woman and police officer
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2020/11.text:
Two members of Austria’s Turkish immigrant community were hailed as heroes after they risked their own lives to rescue an elderly woman and a police officer during the terror attack in Vienna.
Mikail Özen and Recep Gültekin were on their way out for a last coffee before Austria’s new coronavirus lockdown when they heard gunfire.
The two young men, both mixed martial arts (MMA) fighters, rushed to the scene where they found an elderly woman injured.
Mr Gültekin was shot in the leg as they carried her to safety in a nearby restaurant. “When I turned around, the terrorist took aim at me. We came eye to eye,” he told Turkish television.
“I rolled on the ground and ran zigzag to the police station and told them what was happening.”
The two men’s night of drama was not over. As they left the police station shots rang out again. They saw an injured police officer lying motionless on the ground and carried him to safety.
“We didn't think about the danger. We just had to do something. We had to help,” Mr  Özen told Germany’s Bild newspaper.
Footage of the two young men was widley shared on social media and some initially mistook them for terrorists.
But as it became clear what they had done they won widespread praise. “Respect to the two boys from Vienna, Mikail and Recep, who risked their own lives to carry an injured policeman to safety,” Mustafa Durmus, a local politician, tweeted.
“We Muslims of Turkish descent abhor any kind of terror. We stand by Austria, we stand by Vienna. We are always ready to help,” Mr Özen said.

image.caption: Recep Gültekin was shot in the leg as he helped others to safety
Mr Özen (pictured) and Mr Gültekin are both MMA fighters

author: Justin Huggler
